Biryar can decide what each of your listings should cost, explain why,
and, once you switch it on, change the price on Amazon.

It starts switched off. A new listing is not managed, and a new install
cannot change a price at all. Both are on purpose: the whole catalogue
being repriced the moment Amazon is connected is the one default that
could not be taken back.

## What happens in a pass

A pass is one round of pricing. It runs on the schedule you set, and for
each listing you have turned on it does five things:

1. **Reads the market.** Who else sells the product, for how much
   including delivery, and who holds the Featured Offer (the offer behind
   the Add to Cart button).
2. **Works out which situation the listing is in**, and the band of prices
   that situation allows.
3. **Picks a price inside the band.**
4. **Writes down what it decided and why.** That includes deciding to
   change nothing, which is most of the time when things are going well.
5. **Sends the price to Amazon**, if it is allowed to.

The four situations, as the Repricing page names them:

| Situation | What it means |
|---|---|
| Chasing the Featured Offer | Someone else holds it and you are priced above them. Coming down is how it is won. |
| Cheaper, and still not chosen | You are already below the Featured Offer and do not hold it. Price is not the reason, so cutting further would only give money away. |
| Holding the Featured Offer | You hold it. Biryar protects it and tries a little higher, gently. |
| The only seller | Nobody else sells it. The price follows how fast it sells. |

When there is not enough information to tell, Biryar changes nothing.

**The floor.** No price goes below it, ever. It is the higher of two
numbers:

- **Break-even**, worked out from what Amazon really took from your own
  past sales: a percentage plus a fixed charge per unit. It is not taken
  from a fee table. See [How the fees are measured](/methodology/fees/).
- **Your own minimum price** in Seller Central. Amazon refuses to publish
  below it anyway.

Every decision records which of the two set the floor, because they call
for opposite responses. "This would lose money" is a fact about the
product. "Your Seller Central minimum forbids it" is a setting you can
change in a minute.

**The ceiling** is your own maximum price in Seller Central.

A listing with no minimum or maximum in Seller Central cannot be repriced
at all. Biryar will not invent one: that is the one number that is yours
to decide.

## What stops a price from running away

**No big steps.** A single move is never more than 5% of the price.

**No big days.** Small steps add up, so Biryar also watches the whole day.
Once a listing has moved more than 8% from its first price of the day, the
next move waits for you. It appears on the Repricing page under **Waiting
for you**, with Approve and Reject. Restarting Biryar does not reset the
count.

**A price already on its way.** Amazon takes ten minutes and more to
publish a new price. Until the listing shows it, Biryar leaves that
listing alone, for up to 45 minutes, so the same price is not sent twice.

**One last check.** Just before a price is sent, the floor and the ceiling
are checked again, because the market was read a few minutes earlier.

## Approving a move

When a move waits for you, approving it lets the next pass make one move
for that listing. It does not publish the figure you were shown.

That is on purpose. By the time you approve, a competitor may have moved.
So the next pass reads the market again and works out a price for now,
within the same limits. One approval lets one move through.

**The listing**, on the Repricing page. Turn on the ones Biryar may
touch. Every listing is off until you say otherwise.

**The plan.** Sending prices is part of Pro. On the free plan a pass still
runs whenever you start one: it decides, explains and asks Amazon to
check the price, and nothing is applied. That is a preview of exactly
what Pro would do. See [Free and Pro](/plans/).

**Sending prices**, under **Settings, Repricing**. Only an owner can
switch it on. What it means is written beside it: from then on Biryar
changes prices on Amazon while nobody is watching.

Until all three are on, everything else still happens. Each decision made
in that time reads **would have changed, not live**, so you can watch
exactly what would happen, with your real listings and real competitors,
before anything does.

## How often it runs

Under **Settings, Repricing** you choose: every 15 minutes, every hour,
every four hours, once a day, or **Only when I start one**. Running by
itself on a schedule is part of Pro.

**Run a pass now**, on the Repricing page, starts one straight away. The
page shows a pass as it runs: first your listings are read from Amazon,
then each one is priced. It also says when the next pass is due.

If the page says **Queued**, the pass is waiting its turn and starts by
itself. Repricing has its own place in the queue, so a long Sourcing scan
does not hold it up.

## Switching it off

Three ways, from narrow to wide:

- **One listing.** Turn it off on the Repricing page, and only that one
  stops.
- **The schedule.** Under Settings, Repricing, choose **Only when I start
  one**. No pass runs by itself, and every listing keeps its switch for
  when you set a schedule again.
- **Sending.** Turn off sending prices there. Passes still run and decide,
  and nothing is applied.

A price that is already on Amazon stays as it is, whichever you choose.
Biryar never puts an old price back.

## Seeing what it did

**What it decided**, on the Repricing page, lists every decision,
including the ones that changed nothing. A list of changes only would look
the same on a quiet day and on a day when something is broken.

**Price history** shows how one listing's price has moved.

**Learning** shows what the learner, described next, would have done
differently.

## The learner: where to sit inside the band

Working out the band is a rule. You can read it above and disagree with
it. Choosing a price inside the band is a judgement, and the rule's
choice is the middle, which is reasonable and not measured.

So a second part of Biryar learns that choice from your own sales.

### What it learns

It knows five positions in the band: at the floor, a quarter of the way
up, the middle, three quarters, and at the ceiling. It holds one position
for a few days, counts what sold, and works out the profit a day that
position brought. Over time it prefers the positions that earned most with
your products, and now and then tries the others in case the market has
changed.

It learns positions and not prices. A price means nothing next week, once
the competition has moved. "Three quarters of the way up whatever band I
am allowed" still means something. It is also why the learner cannot be
unsafe: a position is always inside the band, and the band is what keeps
the floor. The worst a wrong position can do is earn a little less.

### It starts knowing something

A learner that starts from nothing tries things at random, and with a few
sales a day that would take months. So Biryar comes with a first opinion
about each of the five positions, measured in graded experiments on a real
account.

That opinion is weak on purpose. It is worth about four of your own
experiments, and after that your own results outvote it. It holds three
numbers for each position and nothing else: no prices, no products, no
competitors.

### It prices nothing until you say so

The learner moves through three stages, and only you move it.

| Stage | What it does | What it can tell you |
|---|---|---|
| **Watching** | Notes the price it would have chosen. Publishes nothing. | Whether it is sensible: how often it disagrees with the rule, and by how much. It cannot tell you whether it earns more. |
| **Pricing part of the catalogue** | Prices some of your listings. The rule prices the rest. | Whether it earns more. This is a real measurement. |
| **Pricing everything** | Prices all of them. | |

**Nothing promotes itself.** The Repricing page says whether the results
would support the next stage, and why not when they would not. Moving it
is a button you press. That report is advice and not a lock: you can go
straight to pricing everything, or back to watching after a bad week.

### Why it may say nothing for a while

Three things must be true before an experiment counts. When they are not,
the honest answer is that there is nothing to report yet.

- **The price stayed put long enough.** Anything held for less than half a
  day is not counted.
- **The cost is known.** A listing with no buy price is skipped. It is not
  graded as though the goods were free. See [Portfolio](/guide/portfolio/).
- **The market left it alone.** Where competitors move every hour, no
  price is held long enough to grade, and nothing can be learned there.

## From a terminal

For someone comfortable in a terminal, two commands show the same things
without the page. Neither sends anything to Amazon. Type them in the
`biryar` folder:

```bash
docker compose exec api python -m biryar.catalogue --refresh   # what is listed, and its limits
docker compose exec api python -m biryar.reprice               # what it would charge, and why
```
